newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Kosovo violence clouds Serbian democracy movement.
newsitem.headline: Kosovo violence clouds Serbian democracy movement.

text.p: Renewed political violence in Serbia's Albanian-majority province of Kosovo cast a shadow on Monday over moves by the opposition to break the Socialist Party's autocratic grip on power.

An important development in Serbia's crisis over annulled municipal elections was expected on Monday when a Belgrade court was to announce the outcome of an appeal period after the opposition was declared victorious in the capital.

Two months after the elections, Belgrade's electoral commission decided last week that President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialists (SPS) had lost the capital -- a breakthrough for opposition street protesters.
SPS hardliners vowed to contest the decision in defiance of nine weeks of anti-government demonstrations and pressure from the West, which is threatening to withhold urgent economic aid.
Goran Draganic, an opposition legal adviser, told Reuters on Monday that he had heard the SPS filed an appeal but this could not be confirmed in the run-up to the court announcement.
If no appeal was filed, the court could declare the election result final. If an appeal was lodged, the court could say it had upheld or rejected it, or that it would rule later.
Zajedno wants election victories in 14 major Serbian towns recognised to start democratising Serbia after half a century of effective one-party leftist rule.
But its campaign, backed by Western governments, has been jolted by the potential political fallout of an assassination attempt on a prominent Serb in troubled Kosovo last week.

State-run mainstream media seized on allegations by the SPS mayor of Pristina, Kosovo's main city, that Serbian oppositionists as well as ethnic Albanian separatists plotted to kill the rector of the local university in a car bombing.
The rector was critically injured in the attack but his life is now out of danger, doctors said.
Albanian media published a claim of responsibility for the bombing by the radical Liberation Army of Kosovo.
Pristina Mayor Dusan Simic said "Albanian terrorists" behind the attack "receive support in Belgrade from those who have been trying to destabilise Serbia for two months".
Zajedno leaders condemned the bombing and denied any involvement with it.

But with the influence of SPS-run media still strong outside Belgrade, Zajedno feared that diehard Socialists could exploit the bombing to divert attention from the election imbroglio and invoke some form of state of emergency that could stifle democratic dissent of any kind.
Zajedno said in a statement that the SPS hoped to use the university rector's misfortune to combat Zajedno and distract Serbs from the need to democratise the country.

Anti-government student demonstrators gathered in central Belgrade again on Monday, the 64th day of protests across Serbia, after harrying riot police throughout the night. Tensions were high but no serious incidents were reported.
On Sunday, Zajedno supporters trotted out a new strategy in their often colourful demonstrations, getting hundreds of pet dogs to walk -- and sometimes bark -- for democracy.

Kosovo, whose limited autonomy was revoked by Milosevic in 1989 to quell agitation by its 90 percent Albanian majority for more self-rule and to protect minority Serbs, has been shaken by renewed, sporadic anti-Serb violence in the past year.

Milosevic used attacks on Kosovo Serbs to help centralise and concentrate powers in his hands in the late 1980s and could dust off that strategy now to blunt pressures for democratic change, some analysts say.
Belgrade newspapers said former ultra-nationalist proteges of Milosevic who fought in Bosnia and Croatia in 1992-93 decided in Pristina on Sunday to retaliate against Albanians if attacks continued.
The Serbian Resistance Movement, an opposition group in Kosovo opposed to the Socialists, said in a statement:

"Because things are burning under Milosevic's feet these days, we have reason to believe that the present destabilisation in Kosovo is in the interests of sick minds who can maintain their tyranny in that way alone."
